list.listitem: The history and physical examination are sufficient for a presumptive diagnosis of primary dysmenorrhea in most women. Appropriately evaluate for endometriosis prior to diagnosis. C
Most young women with a clinical presentation consistent with primary dysmenorrhea can be treated empirically with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and/or hormonal contraceptives. A

Nonpharmacologic therapies include topical heat, acupuncture/acupressure, exercise, yoga poses, magnet devices, kinesio taping, and transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS); some herbal therapies appear effective. B
Order pelvic ultrasound and/or refer for laparoscopy in cases of treatment failure. C

background.definition: Dysmenorrhea is painful menses. Primary dysmenorrhea is dysmenorrhea in the absence of any secondary causes such as endometriosis or infection.

list.listitem: Twenty percent to 90% of women of reproductive age experience pain with menses; the variation in this range is largely dependent on the method of assessment.

The highest prevalence, from observational studies, is consistently among adolescents and nulliparous women. In one study of 654 adolescents, 48.9% reported dysmenorrhea of whom only 31.3% responded to NSAIDs or hormonal therapy. Of the 220 remaining girls, 56 had ultrasounds suggestive of endometriosis but only 34 accepted laparoscopy and 27 were confirmed as having endometriosis.

Dysmenorrhea is the most common cause of school absence in adolescent girls; in a study of 250 young women aged 14 to 20 years from 3 family counseling services, 68% had dysmenorrhea, 13% reported limitations in daily activities and 12% lost days of school/work monthly because of dysmenorrhea.

In a case series of young nulliparous women with dysmenorrhea, 46 of 212 dysmenorrhea sufferers tested positive for the dysmenorrhea plus bladder pain phenotype. These women with heightened pelvic sensitivity also reported more non-menstrual pain, dysuria, dyschezia, and dyspareunia compared to women with only dysmenorrhea or control women.

Women with moderate to severe endometriosis-related pain who were clinical responders based on dysmenorrhea and non-menstrual pelvic pain, also experienced significant and clinically meaningful improvement in health-related quality of life and productivity.
There is an association between both dysmenorrhea and menstrual irregularity with pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders.

list.listitem: The Association of Women's Health, Obstetric and Neonatal Nurses recommends asking women if they experience cyclic pelvic pain. No other organizations address screening, and screening should be considered optional. C
The history and physical examination are sufficient for a presumptive diagnosis of primary dysmenorrhea in the majority of cases. C
Laparotomy or laparoscopy with biopsy is the gold standard for diagnosis of endometriosis. C
Ultrasound is useful for the diagnosis of endometriomas and anatomic abnormalities other than endometriosis. B

Pelvic pain not limited to typical location and timing

list.listitem: The typical presentation of primary dysmenorrhea is low anterior pelvic pain with menses that begins shortly after menarche.
Primary dysmenorrhea is typically limited to the timeframe just before the onset of menses for 1 to 3 days.

Physical examination of the abdomen and pelvis should be performed outside the menstrual period to rule out tenderness or obvious mass. Speculum examination and bimanual pelvic examination are optional and often not performed in young adolescents who are not sexually active.
The association between endometriosis and dysmenorrhea is inconsistent. Among infertile women, dysmenorrhea does not reliably distinguish between those with and without endometriosis.
Although findings such as uterosacral pain and nodularityare specific, they are very insensitive (present in only 6%-7% of women).
Diagnostic procedures should be performed if the clinical presentation is not consistent with primary dysmenorrhea or the patient fails drug treatment.
Ultrasound is useful in the diagnosis of ovarian cysts, endometriomas, and some congenital anomalies.
Laparoscopy or laparotomy is the gold standard for diagnosis of endometriosis.
MRI is accurate for the evaluation of adnexal masses and is moderately useful for the diagnosis of advanced stage endometriosis.
Presumptive diagnosis of primary dysmenorrhea may be made on the basis of a typical history and negative physical examination (see for treatment algorithm).
If the history is not typical or there are abnormal physical findings, consider ultrasound, laparoscopy, and/or referral for further evaluation.
NSAIDs and hormonal contraceptives are effective treatments for primary dysmenorrhea. A
Levonorgestrel intrauterine system (Mirena®) reduces primary dysmenorrhea. B

Nonpharmacologic treatments that are probably effective include topical heat, acupuncture/acupressure, exercise, yoga poses, magnet devices, transcutaneous electrical stimulation (TENS), and low-level light therapy. B
Supplements that may be effective include thiamine, vitamin E, magnesium, and fish oil as well as some herbal therapies. B

NSAIDs are well established as effective therapy. Evidence is lacking to demonstrate that any particular NSAID is more effective or safer than others. All NSAIDs have been demonstrated to be more effective than acetaminophen. About one in five women with dysmenorrhea are unresponsive to NSAIDs.

Authors of a network meta-analysis including 35 trials with 4383 participants assessing the efficacy and safety of 5 non-prescription analgesics found all NSAIDs more effective than placebo for treating dysmenorrhea. Aspirin was no more effective than placebo and all drugs had similar safety profiles to placebo. While diclofenac improved pain relief more than ibuprofen and ketoprofen was ranked higher than ibuprofen on the surface under the cumulative ranking area, the authors concluded that, based on efficacy and safety, ibuprofen is the optimal non-prescription drug for primary dysmenorrhea.

A large body of observational data and limited clinical trial evidence indicate that oral contraceptives (OCs) are effective therapy for prevention of dysmenorrhea. Authors of a Cochrane review of 21 RCTs found continuous (>28 days of active hormone) regimens provided better control of menstrual symptoms including pain, than traditional cyclic ones. Bleeding patterns in most studies were similar. Authors of one small RCT found greater subjective pain reduction in the short term (after 1 month) for the continuous regimen but no difference between continuous and cyclic OCs at 6 months.
Hormonal suppression of menses with depo-medroxyprogesterone or extended-cycle OCs prevents dysmenorrhea by definition.
In both a small phase II and phase III trial, the progestin dienogest 1 mg daily produced a greater change from baseline in dysmenorrhea score than placebo at 12 weeks.
Observational data show the levonorgestrel intrauterine device is associated with improvement in both primary dysmenorrhea and secondary dysmenorhhea following surgery for endometriosis.

Treatment of pain associated with secondary dysmenorrhea includes the hormonal approaches described, gonadotropin-releasing hormone agonists, antiprogesterones, and danazol. Evidence to establish one approach as superior to another is lacking.

Authors of a Cochrane review of 5 trials of beta-2 adrenergic agonists (oral isoxsuprine, terbutaline oral spray, ritodrine chloride and oral hydroxyphenyl-orciprenalin) found only one study using combination isoxsuprine, acetaminophen and caffeine demonstrating effectiveness for pain relief. Adverse effects (e.g., nausea, dizziness) occurred in about 25% of patients. The authors concluded that adverse effects make routine use unacceptable.
Cochrane authors found no benefit of infliximab, an anti-tumor necrosis factor-α drug, on pelvic pain reduction in women with endometriosis, based on a single small trial.

For patients with dysmenorrhea from adenomyosis, mifepristone, 10 mg once daily, was shown to improve both the primary outcome of dysmenorrhea and the secondary outcomes of heavy menstrual bleeding and anemia remission at 3 months, based on an RCT including 134 women.
Surgical interruption of pelvic nerve pathways has been insufficiently studied to determine its effectiveness in the treatment of primary or secondary dysmenorrhea.
Radical laparoscopic removal of deep endometriotic lesions has been associated with marked reduction in dysmenorrhea and pelvic pain in a large case series.
Hysterectomy is a last resort if childbearing is complete.
Thiamine 100 mg daily was shown to be an effective treatment for primary dysmenorrhea in a population of young women in India.
Limited evidence suggests that Vitamin E 400 IU daily 5 days per month starting 2 days prior to menses is modestly effective.
Magnesium and omega-3 fatty acids, 2 g daily, show promise but have been insufficiently studied to recommend.
Several small RCTs have demonstrated that 500 mg of ginger root 3 times daily for 5 days starting 2 days prior to onset of menses effectively reduces dysmenorrhea intensity and duration.
In one small RCT, valerian (255 mg three times daily for 3 days at onset of menses) was more effective than placebo on pain severity.
Authors of a systematic review found limited evidence from eight small trials supporting use of Xuefu Zhuyu decoction for dysmenorrhea, but benefit did not reach clinical importance.
Authors of a meta-analysis of 14 RCTs found the Chinese herb Dangguijagyag-san effective for primary dysmenorrhea with a total effective rate of 1.16 (95% CI 1.08-1.24).
The Chinese herbal formula Siwutang was found beneficial for menstrual pain intensity but there was only a single RCT that used a placebo comparison in the 38 studies evaluated.

Cochrane authors found no high quality evidence to support the effectiveness of any dietary supplement for primary dysmenorrhea. There was some low-quality evidence supporting the effectiveness of chamomile, vitamin B1, fenugreek, fish oil, fish oil plus vitamin B1 ginger, valerian, zataria, and zinc sulphate and further study is warranted. Evidence did not support use of vitamin E, dill, guava or fennel.

However, in a meta-analysis of 7 trials at high risk of bias, fennel appeared useful for dysmenorrhea compared to placebo (SMD: -3.27, 95% CI, -5.28 to -1.26) and comparable to conventional drug therapy.

A meta-analysis of 25 trials found both invasive (acupuncture) and especially noninvasive acupoint stimulation more effective than placebo, non-acupoint-related stimulation, or medication on cure rate, effectiveness and pain intensity. Adverse effects of acupuncture (reported in four studies) included local bleeding and hematoma (12%) and needle site pain (10%). However, another systematic review of acupuncture found no evidence of benefit over sham acupuncture in 2 RCTs, and authors of a Cochrane review also concluded that there was insufficient evidence to confirm benefit for either acupuncture or acupressure. Authors of a recent systematic review and meta-analysis found support for use of acupuncture compared to no treatment or NSAIDs.

In one RCT of 221 women with dysmenorrhea comparing smartphone app-delivered self-acupressure with usual care, there was a meaningful reduction of menstrual pain in the intervention group by 6 months with good adherence and continued use by two thirds of the intervention women after the 6th cycle.
Limited evidence suggests that spinal manipulation is ineffective for the treatment of dysmenorrhea.

Authors of a network meta-analysis of 56 RCTs with 5550 subjects found moxibustions (burning dried mugwort) at the navel to be more effective than ibuprofen for dysmenorrhea (OR 6.75, 95% CI, 3.58-13.22).
Aromatherapy (aromatic oil massage with essential oils) appeared to decrease the duration of dysmenorrhea by half a day in one RCT compared with a synthetic fragrance group.
Magnet therapy was effective in one well-designed RCT.
Two RCT's found that yoga programs reduce the severity and duration of primary dysmenorrhea.
A systematic review, including 4 articles and 260 women, demonstrated reduced pain with TENS, as compared to sham therapy (SMD=1.4; 95% CI=0.5, 2.3).

Authors of a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs with 632 women found that exercise reduced menstrual pain intensity by about 25 mm on a 100 mm visual analog scale; benefits on overall menstrual symptoms or quality of life were unclear as these were assessed in only a single trial. Exercise was performed for about 45 to 60 minutes each time, three times weekly or more, and conferred benefit regardless of intensity.

This was essentially confirmed by two more recent meta-analyses. The first analyzed 11 RCTs and reported moderate evidence supporting therapeutic exercise for reducing pain intensity in primary dysmenorrhea with possible benefit on duration of pain and quality of life. The second reported positive effect estimates for physical activity vs comparators for pain intensity (-1.89 cm on visual analog scale; 95% CI, -2.96 to -1.09) and pain duration (-3.92 hours; 95% CI, -4.86 to -2.97) based on 15 eligible RCTs with 1681 participants.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 studies, including the two techniques listed below, concluded that physiotherapy reduced menstrual pain with an MD of -1.13, 95% CI, -1.61 to -0.64, I2 88% (indicating high study heterogeneity).

Kinesio taping on the sacral and suprapubic regions using the ligament technique was superior to sham taping and a control group on pain, anxiety levels, and some menstrual complaints in an RCT of 51 women.
High-frequency TENS is an effective treatment for dysmenorrhea; there are conflicting results regarding the effectiveness of low-frequency TENS.

Topical heat is commonly used for treatment of dysmenorrhea and limited clinical trial evidence suggests it is probably effective. In a Brazilian RCT with 88 women with dysmenorrhea, thermotherapy compared to TENs or placebo reduced pain intensity at 20 minutes, 110 minutes, and 24 hours.
A vibrating tampon (VIPON) was found superior to a single dose of ibuprofen (200-400 mg) for reduction of dysmenorrhea.
A small RCT showed that low level light therapy applied for 20 minutes daily for 5 days showed improvement in dysmenorrhea vs placebo therapy.
Primary dysmenorrhea improves after childbirth. B
In patients with endometriosis, infertility and dysmenorrhea are not highly correlated. However, a diagnosis of endometriosis in adolescents may predict a severe course of disease. B

cell.label: Painful menses; low anterior pelvic pain during 3-day period around start of menses?

Treat with NSAIDs and/or oral contraceptives. Optional suppression of menses with depo-medroxyprogesterone or extended-cycle oral contraceptives. Consider topical heat, acupressure, magnet device, yoga, and/or thiamine, vitamin E, or fish oil. Dysmenorrhea controlled?
Suspect secondary dysmenorrhea; signs or symptoms of sexually transmitted infection?
Consider suppression of menses with depo-medroxyprogesterone or extended-cycle oral contraceptives. Consider surgical options.
